segments.title: How the London Naval Treaty defined little ships
segments.summary: The 1930 London Naval Treaty shows how tonnage, speed, guns, and torpedo equipment separated exempt small vessels from destroyers and cruisers.
segments.body: Articles 8 and 15 of the 1930 London Naval Treaty set the tonnage and armament tests for small warships. Article 8 left Britain room to build ocean-going escorts for minesweeping and anti-submarine work because it did not count depth charges or minesweeping gear among the limiting equipment. Article 15 also helps explain why destroyers clustered below 1,850 tons and used guns under the 5.1-inch threshold. American concern about how Britain might exploit the exemptions helps explain why Article 8 is so detailed. The categories were negotiated rules shaped by national requirements, especially Britain's need for large numbers of escorts.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Articles 8 and 15, their tonnage and weapon limits, and the Royal Navy capabilities left outside aggregate tonnage.

segments.title: Abdiel-class cruisers beat distance with speed and mines
segments.summary: The Abdiel class used 40-knot speed to reach distant passages, lay mines before heavy opposition arrived, and withdraw quickly.
segments.body: The Abdiel-class ships sat awkwardly in treaty categories: at roughly 2,650 tons and armed with six 4-inch guns, they counted as unusually small light cruisers rather than exempt little ships. Their light gun battery also meant they were not intended to trade fire with destroyers or conventional cruisers. Their purpose explains the design. High speed and useful range let them answer the tyranny of distance by racing to a port, passage, or sea line of communication, laying a blocking minefield, and escaping before stronger forces could intervene.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke classifies the Abdiel class and describes its fast offensive minelaying role.

segments.title: HMS Bassett as an ocean-going trawler prototype
segments.summary: HMS Bassett gave the Royal Navy and its partners a compact prewar model for armed trawlers, minesweeping, and anti-submarine duties.
segments.body: Ordered under the Henderson-Goodall program, HMS Bassett provided a working model of an ocean-going vessel below the treaty's 600-ton threshold. At about 529 tons and twelve and a half knots, she showed that a treaty-exempt hull could still perform useful escort work. Her modest gun armament was paired with minesweeping equipment and depth charges, making the design adaptable for British, Canadian, and Indian service. During a reported April 1942 attack by four Messerschmitt Bf 109s, Bassett was said to escape casualties and damage while damaging two attackers. The exact combat score remains a claim in the transcript, while commanders' reports that Bassett withstood bomb damage support the broader point about her robust construction.

evidence.note: The transcript gives Bassett's origins, dimensions, roles, armament, and reported resistance to air attack.

segments.title: Admirable-class minesweepers packed escort weapons into a small hull
segments.summary: The Admirable class combined minesweeping gear, anti-aircraft guns, Hedgehog, and depth charges in a hull whose reported complement of about 104 may be erroneous.
segments.body: At about 625 tons, the Admirable class fell just beyond the treaty's smallest exemption but remained within its broader slow-vessel category. Its dimensions were close to HMS Bassett's, yet the published complement was roughly 104. That figure may be erroneous because it seems unusually high for such a compact hull. The listed equipment still reveals a much denser weapon and minesweeping load: 3-inch and 40 mm guns, 20 mm weapons, Hedgehog, depth-charge gear, and two minesweeping arrangements. Combining anti-aircraft, anti-submarine, and minesweeping duties left very little room aboard, even though the exact crew size remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Admirable-class size and complement with Bassett and lists its extensive armament and minesweeping equipment.

segments.title: Italy's RD-class minesweepers carried an old fleet through another war
segments.summary: The small RD class formed the Regia Marina's most coherent minesweeping group despite interwar age and inconsistent light armament.
segments.body: The roughly 207-ton RD boats were small, lightly crewed, and fitted with whatever armament was available, making exact weapon fits difficult to generalize. Built from 1916 into the 1920s, they belonged to an Italian minesweeping inventory that also included older German and Austro-Hungarian vessels. Although obsolescence reduced the available force by the Second World War, the surviving RD boats still formed the Regia Marina's most homogeneous minesweeping group. Their continued importance shows how specialist auxiliaries can remain operationally essential long after their designs cease to look modern.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke describes RD-class dimensions, uncertain armament, construction history, surviving numbers, and wartime minesweeping importance.

segments.title: Vosper 73-foot boats and the Admiralty fight over coastal strike craft
segments.summary: The Vosper Type I and II pair compact torpedo armament with a procurement struggle over whether small attack craft threatened capital-ship budgets.
segments.body: Britain produced 29 Vosper 73-foot Type I and II boats, but their acquisition became entangled in Admiralty politics. Supporters associated with Reginald Henderson and Stanley Goodall saw value in a treaty-exempt coastal striking force, while opponents feared competition with battleships and carriers. Early in the war, changing the numbers painted on boats helped the Royal Navy suggest that its coastal force was larger than it really was. The Type I carried four 18-inch torpedoes, while the preferred Type II traded two torpedoes for a quick-firing 6-pounder and shifted the design toward heavier gun power.

evidence.note: The transcript covers Vosper production, Admiralty opposition, dimensions, nominal speed, and the armament difference between Types I and II.

segments.title: Elco 80-foot PT boats worked best as ambush predators
segments.summary: PT-109 illustrates how speed, torpedoes, and crew-added weapons made Elco boats dangerous in ambush but vulnerable in a fleet action.
segments.body: The 326 Elco 80-foot boats collectively represented a large torpedo inventory, though a massed charge against a prepared fleet was unrealistic. Radar, gunfire, coordination, and logistics would have made such an attack impractical. Their real strength was as small, fast ambush craft, exemplified by PT-109's four 21-inch torpedoes and a gun battery that crews often augmented in service. Official speed figures for such light craft may also understate what skilled engine crews achieved through wartime tuning and modification.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke uses PT-109 and the Elco production total to contrast unrealistic mass attacks with the boats' effective ambush role.

segments.title: Schnellboots brought greater size and firepower to the torpedo-boat fight
segments.summary: The German Schnellboot combined high speed, reload torpedoes, and multiple cannon in a hull roughly twice the displacement of a Vosper boat.
segments.body: The Allies called German Schnellboots E-boats. They displaced roughly 70 to 100 tons and could make about 43.8 knots. They carried two torpedoes ready in their tubes, two reloads, several 20 mm cannon, and a 37 mm weapon. That combination gave them more sustained torpedo and gun power than the much lighter Vosper boats, even though the practical speed gap could be smaller than official figures imply. The Royal Navy answered them with larger, gun-heavy craft designed for the hunt.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Schnellboot displacement, speed, crew, torpedoes, and cannon with the smaller Vosper boat.

segments.title: Fairmile D dog boats hunted Schnellboots with guns and depth charges
segments.summary: The heavily armed Fairmile D answered the E-boat threat and even used depth-charge blasts to disrupt fast surface targets.
segments.body: The Fairmile D dog boat's heavy guns and frequent use against torpedo boats make its motor-gunboat role clearer than some competing labels. Its battery included 6-pounders, 20 mm Oerlikons, Vickers machine guns, and depth charges, while radar could help crews establish a favorable position against a fast target. Crews could drop depth charges ahead of a pursuing Schnellboot so the underwater blast disrupted or disabled it. The maneuver turned an anti-submarine weapon into a surface-combat trap that left the German boat exposed to gunfire.

evidence.note: The transcript defines the Fairmile D by its gunboat role, lists its weapons, and explains the depth-charge tactic against Schnellboots.

segments.title: Elco S-class gunboats traded torpedoes for concentrated automatic fire
segments.summary: John F. Kennedy's later Elco command shows a Pacific gunboat layout built around machine guns and 40 mm cannon rather than torpedoes.
segments.body: The Elco S-class PTB gunboat displaced about 41 tons and retained a nominal 41-knot speed, but its purpose was expressed through guns rather than torpedoes. John F. Kennedy's second command provides the example of a conversion carrying a dense battery of .50-caliber machine guns, 40 mm cannon, and lighter weapons. Unlike the larger Fairmile D developed to fight Schnellboots in the Channel, this arrangement answered the kinds of Japanese craft encountered in the Pacific. Different opponents and operating areas produced sharply different gunboat solutions from broadly similar fast-boat foundations.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Kennedy's second command and details the Elco S-class gunboat's dimensions, speed, and concentrated gun armament.

segments.title: Spica-class torpedo boats sustained Italy's convoy war
segments.summary: The Spica class combined torpedoes, mines, and strong gun armament in an escort that the Regia Marina depended on for Mediterranean convoys.
segments.body: Although officially torpedo boats, the thousand-ton Spica class carried three 3.9-inch guns, numerous light anti-aircraft weapons, four 18-inch torpedoes, and up to twenty mines. The torpedo-gunboat label reflects how that gun battery made them effective against smaller coastal craft. They were normally outmatched by full destroyers, which brought heavier construction, more guns and torpedoes, and often radar, but that comparison does not make the Spicas unsuccessful ships. Their escort work was indispensable to the Regia Marina's ability to operate and protect convoys in the Mediterranean, while their 100 mm guns made them dangerous opponents for British motor torpedo boats.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke explains his torpedo-gunboat classification and the Spica class's armament, convoy importance, and combat relationship with destroyers.
